reasons.reason: Prices rose by ten percent, and that inflation eats directly into real output, so once the price increase is stripped out of the nominal figures, real GDP ends up falling by the same ten percent.
Dividing each year's nominal GDP by its deflator over 100 gives 500 billion in the first year and 550 divided by 1.1, also 500 billion, in the second, so real output did not move.
A recessionary gap means the economy is producing less than it could at full employment, so the short-run equilibrium sits to the left of the long-run aggregate supply line, below potential output.

A recessionary gap is analysed against the long-run supply curve, and in the long run wages adjust until equilibrium output matches potential GDP, so the model's equilibrium output ends up equal to potential.
The balance of payments has to sum to zero, so when a country spends more abroad than it earns on the current account, the shortfall is financed by net capital inflows, a capital account surplus.
Paying for excess imports sends money out of the country, and money leaving shows up as an outflow on the capital account as well, so the two accounts move together into deficit.
Shrinking the money supply pushes down wages and input prices over time, and lower input costs are exactly what lets firms produce more at each price level, moving short-run aggregate supply outward.

Higher productivity lets firms produce more output with the same labor and capital, lowering per-unit costs, so at every price level they are willing to supply more and the short-run curve moves right.
Borrowing to finance the spending raises interest rates and crowds out an equal amount of private investment, so total demand does not actually change and the price level stays where it was.
At full employment output cannot expand further, so extra government spending adds to aggregate demand against a fixed capacity, and the only thing that can adjust is prices, which rise.

Better production technology raises how much the economy can produce with its existing labor and capital, which increases potential output itself, and potential output is exactly what the long-run supply curve represents.
When consumers demand more goods, firms respond by investing in more capacity to meet that demand, and that added capacity raises how much the economy can produce over the long run.
Oil is an input cost for most firms, so a jump in its price raises production costs everywhere, and firms supply less at each price level, which moves short-run aggregate supply to the left.

When oil gets expensive, households spend much more on fuel and heating and have less left for everything else, and businesses cut spending too, so total spending falls and aggregate demand moves left.
The foreign seller still charges the same amount in its own currency, and the exchange rate does not change what the goods cost to produce, so their price is unaffected by our currency's movement.
When our currency appreciates, each unit of it buys more of the foreign currency, so it takes fewer units of our money to pay the same foreign price, making imported goods cheaper for us.

Stagflation combines stagnation, meaning weak output and rising joblessness, with inflation, so the economy faces high unemployment and high inflation at the same time, which the usual tradeoff says should not happen together.
Stagnation means nothing is moving: wages, prices and hiring all go flat, so inflation stays low and unemployment does not climb either, which leaves both measures sitting at low levels.

Bond sales just move existing savings from buyers to the government, which then spends the money on contracts with private firms, so interest rates hold steady and those firms expand their investment.

Selling bonds to the public raises the government's demand for loanable funds, which pushes up the real interest rate, and that higher cost of borrowing makes firms cancel projects, so private investment falls.
A stronger dollar makes American goods more expensive for buyers paying in euros and makes European goods cheaper for Americans, so exports fall and imports rise, shrinking net exports.
A stronger dollar gives the United States more purchasing power, so American firms buy their inputs abroad more cheaply and can sell more competitively, which lifts the value of net exports.
Heavy government borrowing absorbs the available supply of savings into bonds, bond prices get bid up as investors compete for them, and higher bond prices mean lower interest rates for everyone.

The government's borrowing adds to demand for loanable funds, which raises interest rates, and those higher rates make some private investment unprofitable, so private borrowers are pushed out of the market.

Classical economists assume wages and prices are fully flexible, so any shortfall in demand is corrected by falling wages and prices, and the economy returns on its own to full-employment output in the long run.
In the classical framework fiscal spending is fully offset by crowding out, so the money supply is the only lever left, and the quantity theory ties money directly to nominal spending and output.

A higher federal funds rate rewards saving and draws foreign capital in, and the higher interest income gives households and banks more money to spend, which raises total spending and moves demand rightward.

When consumers feel more confident about their jobs and incomes, they spend more at every price level, and since consumption is the largest part of aggregate demand, the whole curve moves to the right.

With a lower MPC, households save more of each dollar, and those savings flow through banks into new loans and investment, which keeps money circulating and amplifies the effect of government spending.
The spending multiplier equals one over one minus the MPC, so a smaller MPC makes the denominator larger, and each round of spending passes on less income, leaving a smaller multiplier.
